Umbria
UM-bree-uh
n. (the central Italian region of Assisi, Perugia and Spoleto, long part of the papal state and the cradle of the Franciscan movement)
From Latin Umbria, the land of the Umbri, an Italic people east of the Tiber.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Umbria is the landlocked region of central Italy east of Tuscany, the only one of the old Italian regions without a coast. Its towns are hill towns: Perugia, Assisi, Spoleto, Gubbio, Todi, Orvieto, Foligno. For most of the Middle Ages and until 1860 the greater part of Umbria belonged to the papal state, and its history is therefore the history of a Christian population governed directly by churchmen. It produced the Franciscan movement at Assisi, the Benedictine house of Norcia where Benedict was born, and a long succession of mystics, hermits and penitential preachers. It produced very little evangelical reading in the sixteenth century, for the plain reason that the Inquisition in the papal state had no competing jurisdiction to work around. The dictionary records Umbria as the test case of papal government over a devout people. The region was not irreligious; it was intensely religious, and it was also poor, heavily taxed and kept from the Scriptures in its own tongue. Devotion without the text is the condition Umbria illustrates, and the dictionary names it as a real spiritual state rather than a sham, and a dangerous one.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines devotion as a solemn attention to God in worship; a hermit as one who retires from society; penance as the suffering imposed for sin; zeal as ardour in pursuit of an object; and knowledge as a clear perception of truth.

expand to see more

DEVOTION, n. A solemn attention to the Supreme Being in worship; a yielding of the heart and affections to God.

HERMIT, n. A person who retires from society and lives in solitude; a recluse; an anchoret.

PENANCE, n. The suffering, labor or pain to which a person voluntarily subjects himself, or which is imposed on him by authority, as a punishment for his faults.

ZEAL, n. Passionate ardor in the pursuit of any thing; in general, this ardor is a laudable passion.

KNOWLEDGE, n. A clear and certain perception of that which exists, or of truth and fact.

Key Scripture

Rom 10:2 — "For I bear them record that they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge."

Hab 2:14 — "For the earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD, as the waters cover the sea."

Psa 119:130 — "The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple."

Jas 1:22 — "But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves."

Modern Corruption

Landlocked central Italian region of hill towns, long governed directly by the papacy, intensely devout and kept from the Scriptures in its own tongue.

expand to see more

The corruption to name is the sentimental use of Umbria as proof that simple piety is enough and doctrine is for cities. The region was full of devotion, pilgrimage, fasting, and genuine self-denial, and it was kept from the one thing that would have ordered all of it. Paul says exactly this about his own countrymen, with affection and without flattery: “For I bear them record that they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge” (Rom 10:2). The dictionary applies the sentence to a Christian region as readily as to an unbelieving one, because the deficiency is the same.

The second paragraph names the principle to recover, which is that knowledge of God is a thing promised to whole populations and not reserved to clerks. The prophet's expectation is saturation, “For the earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD, as the waters cover the sea” (Hab 2:14), and the instrument is a text that reaches the unlearned: “The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple” (Psa 119:130). James then forbids the opposite error, a people who have the text and treat hearing as the whole duty: “But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves” (Jas 1:22). Umbria's hill towns wanted the first thing and the dictionary wants both for them.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek zelos (G2205), zeal; Greek epignosis (G1922), full knowledge; Hebrew da'ath (H1847), knowledge.

expand to see more

Greek zelos (G2205) — fervour, zeal, ardour; “they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge”, Romans 10:2.

Greek epignosis (G1922) — precise and correct knowledge; “but not according to knowledge”, Romans 10:2.

Hebrew da'ath (H1847) — knowledge, perception; “filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD”, Habakkuk 2:14.

Hebrew pethi (H6612) — simple, untaught, open; “it giveth understanding unto the simple”, Psalm 119:130.

Greek poietes (G4163) — a doer, a performer; “But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only”, James 1:22.

Usage

"“they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge” (Rom 10:2) — the exact condition of devout Umbria."

"“filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD” (Hab 2:14) — the promise that answers it."

"“But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only” (Jas 1:22) — the opposite error, equally named."
